source.text: וַיְהִ֡י בְּאַרְבַּע֩ עֶשְׂרֵ֨ה שָׁנָ֜ה לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ חִזְקִיָּ֗הוּ עָלָ֞ה סַנְחֵרִ֤יב מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֙ עַ֣ל כָּל־עָרֵ֧י יְהוּדָ֛ה הַבְּצֻר֖וֹת וַֽיִּתְפְּשֵֽׂם׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was in [the] fourteen year of king Hezekiah, came up Sennacherib king of Assyria against all [the] cities of Judah the fortified, and seized them.

en.L: And it happened in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah [that] Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and seized them.
en.B: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria marched against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.
en.R: In the fourteenth year that Hezekiah was king, Sennacherib, the king of Assyria, attacked all the walled cities of Judah and captured them.

decisions.choice: Sennacherib king of Assyria: his campaign against Judah in 701 BC
decisions.reason: Sennacherib ruled Assyria from 705 to 681 BC. After Hezekiah rebelled (2 Kings 18:7), Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BC. His own annals claim that he took forty-six of Hezekiah's walled towns and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem, and reliefs from his palace at Nineveh show the siege of Lachish (verse 2). Jerusalem itself was not taken (37:33-37), so "all" means the walled towns of the land.

decisions.choice: the parallel account: 2 Kings 18:13-20:19
decisions.reason: Isaiah 36-39 tells the same events as 2 Kings 18:13-20:19, mostly in the same words. This verse matches 2 Kings 18:13. Isaiah does not have 2 Kings 18:14-16, where Hezekiah pays Sennacherib a heavy tribute of silver and gold; the story goes straight to the officer's arrival at Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: the fourteenth year: dated from Hezekiah's accession
decisions.reason: If the campaign of 701 BC fell in Hezekiah's fourteenth year, his reign began about 715 BC. But 2 Kings 18:9-10 places the fall of Samaria (722 BC) in his sixth year, so the dates for his reign are hard to fit together; some count his years from a time when he shared the throne with Ahaz.

decisions.choice: walled cities
decisions.reason: Readable explains "fortified" as cities with walls.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֣וּר׀אֶת־רַב־שָׁקֵ֨ה מִלָּכִ֧ישׁ יְרוּשָׁלְַ֛מָה אֶל־הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ חִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ בְּחֵ֣יל כָּבֵ֑ד וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֗ד בִּתְעָלַת֙ הַבְּרֵכָ֣ה הָעֶלְיוֹנָ֔ה בִּמְסִלַּ֖ת שְׂדֵ֥ה כוֹבֵֽס׃

records.literal_gloss: And sent [the] king of Assyria [the] Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem to the king Hezekiah with an army heavy, and he stood at [the] conduit of the pool the upper on [the] highway of [the] field of [the] washer.

en.L: And the king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah, with a heavy army, and he stood at the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway to the Fuller's Field.
en.B: Then the king of Assyria sent the chief officer from Lachish to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah, with a large army. The officer took his stand by the water channel from the Upper Pool, on the road to the Fuller's Field.
en.R: The king of Assyria was at the city of Lachish. From there he sent the Assyrian commander to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem with a large army. The commander stood by the water channel that comes from the Upper Pool. It is on the road to the field where cloth is washed.

decisions.choice: Rabshakeh: the title of a high Assyrian official, not a personal name
decisions.reason: The word is an Assyrian title, made of "chief" and an office usually taken to mean "cupbearer"; by this time it named one of the king's highest officers, able to command troops and speak for the king. The text never gives the man's name. In 2 Kings 18:17 he comes with two other officials, also named by their titles.

decisions.choice: Lachish: the chief city of Judah after Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Lachish lay in the hills about 30 miles southwest of Jerusalem. Sennacherib besieged it himself (2 Chronicles 32:9), and carved scenes of its capture on the walls of his palace at Nineveh. He was still there when he sent his officer to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: the conduit of the upper pool: the place where Isaiah met Ahaz
decisions.reason: The officer stands at the very spot named in 7:3, where Isaiah met King Ahaz and urged him to trust the LORD instead of seeking help; Ahaz turned to Assyria (2 Kings 16:7). The parallel in 2 Kings 18:17 names the place in the same words.

decisions.choice: the Rabshakeh
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Assyrian title as a title, with the article, as the Hebrew has it. Chapter 37 follows the same wording.

decisions.choice: the chief officer
decisions.reason: Balanced translates the title instead of keeping it as a strange name. The traditional "Rabshakeh" reads like a personal name, which it is not.

decisions.choice: the Assyrian commander
decisions.reason: Readable names the man by what he did: he led the Assyrian army to Jerusalem and spoke for the king.

decisions.choice: The king of Assyria was at the city of Lachish. From there he sent ...
decisions.reason: Readable says first where the king was, then sends the commander, to keep the sentences short.

source.text: וַיֵּצֵ֥א אֵלָ֛יו אֶלְיָקִ֥ים בֶּן־חִלְקִיָּ֖הוּ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל־הַבָּ֑יִת וְשֶׁבְנָא֙ הַסֹּפֵ֔ר וְיוֹאָ֥ח בֶּן־אָסָ֖ף הַמַּזְכִּֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: And went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah who [was] over the house, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder.

en.L: And Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who [was] over the house, went out to him, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder.
en.B: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, went out to him, together with Shebna the secretary and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder.
en.R: Three of Hezekiah's officials went out to meet him. They were Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the king's palace, Shebna, the royal secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, who kept the records.

decisions.choice: Eliakim over the house, Shebna the secretary
decisions.reason: In 22:15-25 Shebna was over the house and the LORD said Eliakim son of Hilkiah would take his post. Here Eliakim holds that office and Shebna serves as secretary.

decisions.choice: secretary and recorder: senior royal officials
decisions.reason: The secretary handled the king's letters and records of state; the recorder (literally "one who causes to remember") kept official records and perhaps announced the king's decisions. Both offices appear among David's officials (2 Samuel 8:16-17).

decisions.choice: they went out to him
decisions.reason: In 2 Kings 18:18 the Assyrians first call for the king, and these three officials go out in his place. Isaiah tells it more briefly.

decisions.choice: Three of Hezekiah's officials ... They were ...
decisions.reason: Readable says first who the men were, then lists them, and explains "recorder" as the one who kept the records.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶם֙ רַב־שָׁקֵ֔ה אִמְרוּ־נָ֖א אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ הַגָּדוֹל֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר מָ֧ה הַבִּטָּח֛וֹן הַזֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּטָֽחְתָּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to them [the] Rabshakeh, say please to Hezekiah, thus says the king the great, [the] king of Assyria, what [is] the trust the this which you trust?

en.L: And the Rabshakeh said to them, "Say, please, to Hezekiah, 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: What [is] this trust that you trust?
en.B: Then the chief officer said to them, "Tell Hezekiah, 'The great king, the king of Assyria, says this: What sort of confidence is this that you are trusting in?
en.R: Then the Assyrian commander said to them, "Give Hezekiah this message: 'This is what the great king, the king of Assyria, says: Why do you feel so safe?

decisions.choice: the great king: a title of the kings of Assyria
decisions.reason: Assyrian kings called themselves "the great king, king of the world", ruler over lesser kings. Here the title is set against Hezekiah, whom the officer never calls king (verses 4, 14).

decisions.choice: trust: the ground of Hezekiah's confidence
decisions.reason: The noun and the verb come from the same root, which runs through the speech (verses 5, 6, 7, 9, 15): what is Hezekiah relying on? The officer offers three answers and mocks each: Egypt (verse 6), the LORD (verse 7), Judah's own strength (verses 8-9).

decisions.choice: the king's message runs to the end of verse 10
decisions.reason: The officer speaks as the king's messenger: the whole of verses 4-10 is the message he was sent to give, though in verse 8 he speaks of "my master" in his own voice.

decisions.choice: What sort of confidence is this that you are trusting in?
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps both the noun and the verb of trust, as the Hebrew does.

decisions.choice: Why do you feel so safe?
decisions.reason: Readable puts the question about trust in plain words.

source.text: אָמַ֨רְתִּי֙ אַךְ־דְּבַר־שְׂפָתַ֔יִם עֵצָ֥ה וּגְבוּרָ֖ה לַמִּלְחָמָ֑ה עַתָּה֙ עַל־מִ֣י בָטַ֔חְתָּ כִּ֥י מָרַ֖דְתָּ בִּֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: I say, only a word of lips [is] counsel and strength for war. Now on whom do you rely that you have rebelled against me?

en.L: I say, only a word of lips [is your] counsel and might for war. Now, on whom do you rely, that you have rebelled against me?
en.B: I tell you, your strategy and your strength for war are nothing but empty words. Who is it you are leaning on, that you have rebelled against me?
en.R: I say that your plans and your power for war are only empty talk. Who are you depending on that makes you turn against me?

decisions.choice: I say: the king calls Judah's war plans empty talk
decisions.reason: The Masoretic Text reads "I say". The parallel in 2 Kings 18:20 reads "you say", one letter different, so that the king mocks Hezekiah's claim: "you say you have a plan and strength for war, but it is only words." The Great Isaiah Scroll is reported to read "you say" here as well. The sense is nearly the same either way: Judah's preparations are mere talk.

decisions.choice: a word of lips: empty talk, words with nothing behind them
decisions.reason: The same phrase is used in Proverbs 14:23: mere talk leads only to poverty.

decisions.choice: rebelled: Hezekiah stopped paying tribute to Assyria
decisions.reason: Judah had paid tribute to Assyria since Ahaz (2 Kings 16:7-8). Hezekiah "rebelled against the king of Assyria and did not serve him" (2 Kings 18:7), most likely after Sargon's death in 705 BC.

decisions.choice: your strategy and your strength for war are nothing but empty words
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the subject first and supplies "your", which the context makes plain.

source.text: הִנֵּ֣ה בָטַ֡חְתָּ עַל־מִשְׁעֶנֶת֩ הַקָּנֶ֨ה הָרָצ֤וּץ הַזֶּה֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִסָּמֵ֥ךְ אִישׁ֙ עָלָ֔יו וּבָ֥א בְכַפּ֖וֹ וּנְקָבָ֑הּ כֵּ֚ן פַּרְעֹ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־מִצְרַ֔יִם לְכָֽל־הַבֹּטְחִ֖ים עָלָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: Look, you rely on [the] staff of the reed the crushed the this, on Egypt, which leans a man on it and it goes into his palm and pierces it. So [is] Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who rely on him.

en.L: Look, you rely on the staff of this crushed reed, on Egypt, on which [if] a man leans, it will go into his palm and pierce it. So [is] Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who rely on him.
en.B: Look, you are leaning on Egypt, this cracked reed you use for a staff. Anyone who puts weight on it will have it run into the hand and pierce it. That is what Pharaoh king of Egypt is to all who rely on him.
en.R: Look! You are depending on Egypt to help you. But Egypt is like a walking stick made from a cracked reed. If you lean on it, it will split and stab into your hand. That is what Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is like for everyone who depends on him.

decisions.choice: the staff of this crushed reed: Egypt, a support that fails and wounds
decisions.reason: Reeds grew along the Nile. A cracked reed used as a walking stick gives way and its split end stabs the hand that leans on it. Ezekiel 29:6-7 uses the same picture of Egypt.

decisions.choice: Egypt and Pharaoh: Judah's hoped-for ally
decisions.reason: Egypt was then ruled by kings from Cush (37:9). Isaiah had warned Judah against looking to Egypt for help (30:1-7; 31:1-3); here the enemy says the same thing for his own reasons.

decisions.choice: depending on Egypt to help you
decisions.reason: Readable adds "to help you" and spells out that Egypt is like the cracked reed.

source.text: וְכִי־תֹאמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖ינוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲלוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣יו וְאֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔יו וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽיהוּדָה֙ וְלִיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִפְנֵ֛י הַמִּזְבֵּ֥חַ הַזֶּ֖ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֽוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And if you say to me, to Yahweh our God we trust, [is] not he [the one] whose removed Hezekiah his high places and his altars, and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, before the altar the this you will bow down?

en.L: And if you say to me, "In {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} our God we trust," [is] not {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} [the one] whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah has removed, and has said to Judah and to Jerusalem, "Before this altar you shall bow down"?
en.B: Or if you tell me, "Our trust is in {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} our God," did Hezekiah not get rid of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} high places and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} altars? Did he not tell Judah and Jerusalem, "It is before this altar that you must bow down"?
en.R: Maybe you will tell me, "We are trusting {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} our God." But Hezekiah tore down {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s places of worship on the hills and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} altars. He told the people of Judah and Jerusalem, "You must worship only at this one altar in Jerusalem."

decisions.choice: Hezekiah removed the high places: his reform of worship
decisions.reason: Hezekiah removed the high places, local shrines on hills, and their altars, and called the people to worship at the temple in Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:4, 22; 2 Chronicles 31:1), as Deuteronomy 12:5-14 commands. The officer treats this as an insult to the LORD, as if Hezekiah had robbed his own God of worship.

decisions.choice: if you say: the parallel in 2 Kings 18:22
decisions.reason: Here the verb is singular, spoken to Hezekiah through his officials; in 2 Kings 18:22 it is plural, "if you all say". Kings also ends the verse "in Jerusalem".

decisions.choice: did Hezekiah not get rid of his high places and his altars? Did he not tell ...
decisions.reason: Balanced turns the one long question into two shorter ones with Hezekiah as the subject.

decisions.choice: places of worship on the hills ... only at this one altar in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable explains the high places and spells out what "this altar" meant: the altar of the temple in Jerusalem, now the only place for sacrifice.

source.text: וְעַתָּה֙ הִתְעָ֣רֶב נָ֔א אֶת־אֲדֹנִ֖י הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְאֶתְּנָ֤ה לְךָ֙ אַלְפַּ֣יִם סוּסִ֔ים אִם־תּוּכַ֕ל לָ֥תֶת לְךָ֖ רֹכְבִ֥ים עֲלֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And now make a wager please with my master the king of Assyria, and let me give to you two thousand horses, if you are able to put for yourself riders on them.

en.L: And now, make a wager, please, with my master the king of Assyria, and I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to put riders on them.
en.B: Come, then, place a bet with my master the king of Assyria. I will hand you two thousand horses, if you can supply men to ride them!
en.R: Let me make a deal with you on behalf of my master, the king of Assyria. If you can find two thousand men to ride them, I will give you two thousand horses!

decisions.choice: make a wager: exchange pledges, take up a challenge
decisions.reason: The verb means to give a pledge or to enter into an agreement (Genesis 43:9; Proverbs 20:19 uses a related sense). Here it is a mocking bet: Judah could not take up the offer.

decisions.choice: two thousand horses: a taunt about Judah's weakness
decisions.reason: Assyria's army was famous for its horsemen and chariots. The officer mocks Judah as too weak even to find two thousand trained riders. Isaiah had warned against trusting in horses (31:1).

decisions.choice: my master: the officer speaks in his own voice
decisions.reason: Inside the king's message (verses 4-10) the officer speaks of "my master", so the king's words and his own run together.

decisions.choice: two thousand men
decisions.reason: Readable repeats the number to make the taunt plain.

source.text: וְאֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖י הַקְטַנִּ֑ים וַתִּבְטַ֤ח לְךָ֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם לְרֶ֖כֶב וּלְפָרָשִֽׁים׃

records.literal_gloss: And how will you turn back the face of a governor, one of the servants of my master the least, and you trust for yourself on Egypt for chariotry and for horsemen?

en.L: And how will you turn back the face of one governor [among] the least of my master's servants, and you rely on Egypt for chariots and for horsemen?
en.B: Then how could you drive off a single governor, one of my master's lowest officials? Yet you put your trust in Egypt to send chariots and horsemen!
en.R: You could not even defeat one of my master's least important officers. So why do you trust Egypt to give you chariots and horsemen?

decisions.choice: turn back the face: drive back, repel
decisions.reason: To turn back someone's face can mean to refuse a request (1 Kings 2:16), but here it means to make an enemy retreat.

decisions.choice: governor: an Assyrian provincial official
decisions.reason: The word, borrowed from Assyrian, names a governor of a province. Even one of the least of these officials, the officer says, is more than Judah can face.

decisions.choice: and you rely on Egypt: a mocking contrast
decisions.reason: The clause states the absurdity: Judah cannot face one minor official, yet hopes Egypt's chariots will save it.

decisions.choice: officials / officers
decisions.reason: The king's servants here are his officials, as elsewhere for court officials.

source.text: וְעַתָּה֙ הֲמִבַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הָאָ֥רֶץ הַזֹּ֖את לְהַשְׁחִיתָ֑הּ יְהוָה֙ אָמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔י עֲלֵ֛ה אֶל־הָאָ֥רֶץ הַזֹּ֖את וְהַשְׁחִיתָֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And now, [is it] without Yahweh [that] I have come up against the land the this to destroy it? Yahweh said to me, go up against the land the this and destroy it.

en.L: And now, [is it] apart from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [that] I have come up against this land to destroy it? {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to me, "Go up against this land and destroy it."'"
en.B: And was it apart from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that I came up to ruin this land? It was {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} who said to me, "Go up against this land and ruin it."'"
en.R: Do you think I came to destroy this land without the permission of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? It was {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} who told me, "Attack this land and destroy it!"'"

decisions.choice: the LORD said to me: the king claims the LORD's backing
decisions.reason: The claim is the Assyrian's, meant to shake Judah's trust. It holds a twisted truth: in 10:5-15 the LORD calls Assyria the rod of his anger against his people, but condemns the king who boasts as if he acted by his own strength. Chapter 37 answers the boast (37:23-29).

decisions.choice: destroy: ruin, lay waste
decisions.reason: The verb is used for ruining a land or a city in war (Genesis 19:13; Jeremiah 36:29).

decisions.choice: without the permission of the LORD
decisions.reason: Readable explains "without the LORD" as acting without his permission.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶלְיָקִים֩ וְשֶׁבְנָ֨א וְיוֹאָ֜ח אֶל־רַב־שָׁקֵ֗ה דַּבֶּר־נָ֤א אֶל־עֲבָדֶ֨יךָ֙ אֲרָמִ֔ית כִּ֥י שֹׁמְעִ֖ים אֲנָ֑חְנוּ וְאַל־תְּדַבֵּ֤ר אֵלֵ֨ינוּ֙ יְהוּדִ֔ית בְּאָזְנֵ֣י הָעָ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֖ר עַל־הַחוֹמָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Eliakim and Shebna and Joah to [the] Rabshakeh, speak please to your servants Aramaic, for understanding [are] we, and do not speak to us Judean in the ears of the people who [are] on the wall.

en.L: And Eliakim and Shebna and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, "Speak, please, to your servants [in] Aramaic, for we understand [it]; and do not speak to us [in] Judean in the ears of the people who [are] on the wall."
en.B: Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the chief officer, "We beg you, use Aramaic when you talk with your servants, because we know it. Do not talk to us in the language of Judah while the people on the wall are listening."
en.R: Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Assyrian commander, "Please speak to us in Aramaic. We understand it. Do not speak to us in Hebrew, the language of Judah. The people on the city wall are listening."

decisions.choice: Aramaic: the shared language of diplomacy
decisions.reason: Aramaic was spoken across Syria and used throughout the Assyrian empire for letters and treaties. Judah's officials knew it; ordinary people in Jerusalem did not. Later Ezra 4:7 and Daniel 2:4 contain Aramaic.

decisions.choice: Judean: the language of Judah, Hebrew
decisions.reason: The word names the Hebrew spoken in Judah (Nehemiah 13:24). The officials want the talks kept from the soldiers and people listening on the wall, who would understand every threat.

decisions.choice: your servants: a polite way of saying "us"
decisions.reason: Speaking of oneself as the other's servant was a courteous form of address.

decisions.choice: us ... Hebrew, the language of Judah
decisions.reason: Readable says "us" for the polite "your servants" and gives the language its familiar name.

decisions.choice: the language of Judah
decisions.reason: Balanced explains the word as the language of Judah, since "Judean" alone is not a familiar language name.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר רַב־שָׁקֵ֗ה הַאֶ֨ל אֲדֹנֶ֤יךָ וְאֵלֶ֨יךָ֙ שְׁלָחַ֣נִי אֲדֹנִ֔י לְדַבֵּ֖ר אֶת־הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה הֲלֹ֣א עַל־הָאֲנָשִׁ֗ים הַיֹּֽשְׁבִים֙ עַל־הַ֣חוֹמָ֔ה לֶאֱכֹ֣ל אֶת־צוֹאָתָ֗ם וְלִשְׁתּ֛וֹת אֶת־מֵימֵ֥י רַגְלֵיהֶ֖ם עִמָּכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] Rabshakeh, [is it] to your master and to you [that] has sent me my master to speak the words the these? [Is it] not to the men sitting on the wall, to eat their excrement and to drink the water of their feet with you?

en.L: But the Rabshakeh said, "[Is it] to your master and to you [that] my master has sent me to speak these words? [Is it] not to the men who sit on the wall, to eat their own excrement and to drink the water of their feet with you?"
en.B: But the chief officer replied, "Did my master send me to speak these words just to you and your master? No, they are for the men who sit on the wall, who are going to eat their own dung and drink their own urine along with you!"
en.R: But the Assyrian commander said, "My master did not send me to say these things only to you and your master. He sent me to speak to the men sitting on the wall too. When we surround the city, they will have to eat their own waste and drink their own urine, just like you."

decisions.choice: their excrement ... the water of their feet: the words read aloud
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text have two blunter words for dung and urine. The Masoretic reading tradition (the qere) replaces them, when read aloud, with the milder "their excrement" and "the water of their feet". The meaning is the same; only the coarseness differs. The parallel in 2 Kings 18:27 has the same pair of readings.

decisions.choice: the water of their feet: urine
decisions.reason: A polite way of naming urine; "feet" is used for the lower body (compare 7:20).

decisions.choice: to eat and drink with you: the hunger of a long siege
decisions.reason: The threat is that a siege will bring the city to such hunger and thirst that people are driven to eat and drink filth (compare 2 Kings 6:25). The men on the wall will share that fate with their leaders.

decisions.choice: When we surround the city
decisions.reason: Readable states that the threat is about a siege, which the Hebrew leaves the hearers to supply.

source.text: וַֽיַּעֲמֹד֙ רַב־שָׁקֵ֔ה וַיִּקְרָ֥א בְקוֹל־גָּד֖וֹל יְהוּדִ֑ית וַיֹּ֕אמֶר שִׁמְע֗וּ אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֛י הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ הַגָּד֖וֹל מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר׃

records.literal_gloss: And stood [the] Rabshakeh and called with a voice great [in] Judean and said, hear the words of the king the great, the king of Assyria.

en.L: And the Rabshakeh stood and called out with a loud voice [in] Judean, and said, "Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!
en.B: Then the chief officer stood and shouted in the language of Judah: "Listen to the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!
en.R: Then the Assyrian commander stood and shouted loudly in Hebrew, "Listen to what the great king, the king of Assyria, says!

decisions.choice: stood and called out in Judean: he does the opposite of what was asked
decisions.reason: Instead of moving to Aramaic, the officer takes his stand and shouts in the people's own language, now speaking past the officials to the people on the wall. His speech runs to the end of verse 20.

decisions.choice: Hebrew
decisions.reason: Readable gives the language of Judah its familiar name, as in verse 11.

source.text: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אַל־יַשִּׁ֥א לָכֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּ֥י לֹֽא־יוּכַ֖ל לְהַצִּ֥יל אֶתְכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Thus says the king, let not deceive you Hezekiah, for not he will be able to deliver you.

en.L: Thus says the king: 'Let not Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you.
en.B: The king says this: 'Do not let Hezekiah fool you. He has no power to rescue you.
en.R: This is what the king says: 'Do not let Hezekiah trick you. He cannot save you.

decisions.choice: deliver: rescue from an enemy's power
decisions.reason: The verb "deliver" is the key word of verses 14-20, used seven times: Hezekiah cannot deliver, the LORD will not, and no god has. Chapter 37 shows who can.

decisions.choice: deliver you: the parallel in 2 Kings 18:29
decisions.reason: Kings has "deliver you from his hand", with the king of Assyria speaking of himself in the third person. Isaiah has a shorter text.

decisions.choice: rescue / save
decisions.reason: Balanced says "rescue" and Readable "save" for the verb "deliver" all through verses 14-20, so the repeated word stays repeated.

source.text: וְאַל־יַבְטַ֨ח אֶתְכֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה לֵאמֹ֔ר הַצֵּ֥ל יַצִּילֵ֖נוּ יְהוָ֑ה לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ הָעִ֣יר הַזֹּ֔את בְּיַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר׃

records.literal_gloss: And let not make you trust Hezekiah in Yahweh, saying, surely will deliver us Yahweh; not will be given the city the this into [the] hand of [the] king of Assyria.

en.L: And let not Hezekiah make you trust in {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, saying, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria."'
en.B: And do not let Hezekiah lead you to rely on {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} when he tells you, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is sure to rescue us. The king of Assyria will never be given this city."'
en.R: Do not let him talk you into trusting {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. He says, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will surely save us. The king of Assyria will not be allowed to capture this city."'

decisions.choice: make you trust: cause you to rely
decisions.reason: The verb is the causing form of "trust", the word that runs through the speech (verse 4). The officer admits that Hezekiah is calling the people to trust the LORD.

decisions.choice: this city will not be given: the promise the LORD keeps
decisions.reason: The officer quotes Hezekiah's confidence to mock it. The LORD's answer in 37:33-35 and 38:6 is that he will defend this city.

decisions.choice: will not be allowed to capture
decisions.reason: Readable puts "given into the hand of" as being allowed to capture.

source.text: אַֽל־תִּשְׁמְע֖וּ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּסכִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֜ר הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֗וּר עֲשֽׂוּ־אִתִּ֤י בְרָכָה֙ וּצְא֣וּ אֵלַ֔י וְאִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ־גַּפְנוֹ֙ וְאִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵנָת֔וֹ וּשְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵי־בוֹרֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Do not listen to Hezekiah, for thus says the king of Assyria, make with me a blessing and come out to me, and eat each his vine and each his fig tree, and drink each [the] water of his cistern,

en.L: Do not listen to Hezekiah, for thus says the king of Assyria: 'Make a blessing with me and come out to me, and eat each [from] his vine and each [from] his fig tree, and drink each the water of his cistern,
en.B: Do not listen to Hezekiah. The king of Assyria says this: 'Come to terms with me and surrender to me. Then everyone may eat from their own vine and their own fig tree and drink water from their own cistern,
en.R: Do not listen to Hezekiah. The king of Assyria says this: 'Make peace with me. Come out of the city and give yourselves up to me. Then each of you can eat grapes from your own vine and figs from your own fig tree. You can drink water from your own well.

decisions.choice: make a blessing with me: make peace, come to terms
decisions.reason: "Blessing" here is a peace agreement, perhaps sealed with a gift; the word can mean a gift (1 Samuel 25:27; 2 Kings 5:15).

decisions.choice: come out to me: surrender
decisions.reason: To come out to a besieging king meant to open the gates and give up (1 Samuel 11:3; Jeremiah 38:17).

decisions.choice: each under his vine and fig tree: a picture of peace
decisions.reason: To enjoy one's own vine and fig tree describes peace and safety (Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10). The Assyrian king offers what only the LORD truly gives.

decisions.choice: well
decisions.reason: Readable says "well" for a cistern, a pit cut in rock to store rainwater.

source.text: עַד־בֹּאִ֕י וְלָקַחְתִּ֥י אֶתְכֶ֖ם אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּאַרְצְכֶ֑ם אֶ֤רֶץ דָּגָן֙ וְתִיר֔וֹשׁ אֶ֥רֶץ לֶ֖חֶם וּכְרָמִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: until I come and take you to a land like your land, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards.

en.L: until I come and take you to a land like your land, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards.
en.B: until I come to move you to a country like your own, a country of grain and fresh wine, of bread and vineyards.
en.R: You can do this until I come and take you away to another country. It will be like your own country. It will have plenty of grain and wine, bread and vineyards.

decisions.choice: take you to a land: deportation
decisions.reason: Assyria moved conquered peoples from their homelands to other parts of the empire, as it had done with Israel after Samaria fell (2 Kings 17:6, 24). The promise of a good land describes exile.

decisions.choice: the parallel in 2 Kings 18:32
decisions.reason: Kings continues the list: "a land of olive oil and honey, so that you may live and not die".

decisions.choice: You can do this until ...
decisions.reason: Readable begins a new sentence and repeats what the people may do until the king comes.

source.text: פֶּן־יַסִּ֨ית אֶתְכֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר יְהוָ֖ה יַצִּילֵ֑נוּ הַהִצִּ֜ילוּ אֱלֹהֵ֤י הַגּוֹיִם֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־אַרְצ֔וֹ מִיַּ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר׃

records.literal_gloss: lest mislead you Hezekiah, saying, Yahweh will deliver us. Have delivered the gods of the nations each his land from [the] hand of [the] king of Assyria?

en.L: [Beware] lest Hezekiah mislead you, saying, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will deliver us." Have the gods of the nations delivered, each his land, from the hand of the king of Assyria?
en.B: Watch out, or Hezekiah will lead you astray by saying, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will rescue us." Did any of the gods of the nations ever rescue its own land from the hand of the king of Assyria?
en.R: Do not let Hezekiah fool you when he says, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will save us." Has the god of any other nation ever saved its country from the king of Assyria?

decisions.choice: the gods of the nations: the LORD counted as one god among many
decisions.reason: The officer sets the LORD alongside the gods of conquered peoples. Hezekiah answers this in his prayer: those gods were "not gods" but the work of human hands, and the LORD alone is God (37:18-20).

decisions.choice: lest: a warning that follows on from verse 16
decisions.reason: The word means "so that not" and carries on the warning "Do not listen to Hezekiah".

source.text: אַיֵּ֞ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י חֲמָת֙ וְאַרְפָּ֔ד אַיֵּ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֣י סְפַרְוָ֑יִם וְכִֽי־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־שֹׁמְר֖וֹן מִיָּדִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Where [are] the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where [are] the gods of Sepharvaim? And have they delivered Samaria from my hand?

en.L: Where [are] the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where [are] the gods of Sepharvaim? And have they delivered Samaria from my hand?
en.B: Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Did they rescue Samaria from my hand?
en.R: What happened to the gods of the cities of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Did any god save the city of Samaria from me?

decisions.choice: Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim: places Assyria had conquered
decisions.reason: Hamath and Arpad were cities of Syria taken by Assyria in the years before (10:9). People from Sepharvaim were settled in Samaria after its fall (2 Kings 17:24, 31); where it lay is not known for certain.

decisions.choice: Samaria: the capital of Israel, taken in 722 BC
decisions.reason: Samaria fell to Assyria after a three-year siege, and Israel's people were deported (2 Kings 17:5-6). It worshiped the LORD in name, yet was not spared (10:10-11).

decisions.choice: the parallel in 2 Kings 18:34
decisions.reason: Kings adds "Hena and Ivvah" to the list, and the question about Samaria may be read there as "have they delivered Samaria"; here "they" are the gods just named or any gods at all.

source.text: מִ֗י בְּכָל־אֱלֹהֵ֤י הָֽאֲרָצוֹת֙ הָאֵ֔לֶּה אֲשֶׁר־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־אַרְצָ֖ם מִיָּדִ֑י כִּֽי־יַצִּ֧יל יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם מִיָּדִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Who among all [the] gods of the lands the these [are those] who have delivered their land from my hand, that should deliver Yahweh Jerusalem from my hand?

en.L: Who among all the gods of these lands [are those] who have delivered their land from my hand, that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} should deliver Jerusalem from my hand?'"
en.B: Among all the gods of these countries, which ones have rescued their land from my hand, that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} should rescue Jerusalem from me?'"
en.R: None of the gods of these countries has saved its land from me. So how could {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} save Jerusalem from me?'"

decisions.choice: that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem: the boast the LORD answers
decisions.reason: This is the high point of the speech: the LORD is just another god who will fail. In 37:23 the LORD calls this mocking an insult to the Holy One of Israel, and in 37:36 he delivers the city.

decisions.choice: None of the gods ... has saved ... So how could ...
decisions.reason: Readable turns the first rhetorical question into the statement it implies.

source.text: וַֽיַּחֲרִ֔ישׁוּ וְלֹֽא־עָנ֥וּ אֹת֖וֹ דָּבָ֑ר כִּֽי־מִצְוַ֨ת הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ הִ֛יא לֵאמֹ֖ר לֹ֥א תַעֲנֻֽהוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And they kept silent and not answered him a word, for [the] command of the king it [was], saying, not you shall answer him.

en.L: And they kept silent and did not answer him a word, for the king's command was, "Do not answer him."
en.B: They stayed silent and did not say a word in reply, for the king had given an order: "Do not answer him."
en.R: But everyone stayed silent. No one answered him, because King Hezekiah had commanded, "Do not answer him."

decisions.choice: they kept silent: the officials and the people on the wall
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject. The parallel in 2 Kings 18:36 says "the people kept silent". The three officials kept silent as well, as the king had commanded.

decisions.choice: everyone ... King Hezekiah
decisions.reason: Readable names who kept silent and which king gave the order.

source.text: וַיָּבֹ֣א אֶלְיָקִ֣ים בֶּן־חִלְקִיָּ֣הוּ אֲשֶׁר־עַל־הַ֠בַּיִת וְשֶׁבְנָ֨א הַסּוֹפֵ֜ר וְיוֹאָ֨ח בֶּן־אָסָ֧ף הַמַּזְכִּ֛יר אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ קְרוּעֵ֣י בְגָדִ֑ים וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ ל֔וֹ אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֥י רַב־שָׁקֵֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And came Eliakim son of Hilkiah who [was] over the house, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder, to Hezekiah [with] torn clothes, and they told him the words of [the] Rabshakeh.

en.L: And Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who [was] over the house, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder came to Hezekiah [with] torn clothes, and they told him the words of the Rabshakeh.
en.B: Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported to him what the chief officer had said.
en.R: Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, who kept the records, went to Hezekiah. They had torn their clothes to show their grief. They told him everything the Assyrian commander had said.

decisions.choice: torn clothes: a sign of grief and alarm
decisions.reason: Tearing one's clothes showed deep distress (Genesis 37:29; 2 Kings 18:37). Hezekiah does the same when he hears their report (37:1).

decisions.choice: to show their grief
decisions.reason: Readable explains why they tore their clothes.
